overview: The Samanid Empire sparked the revival of Persian language and culture after two centuries of Arab dominance. Centered in Bukhara, it patronized scholars, poets and scientists who laid the foundations of the Islamic Golden Age in Central Asia.

items.text: Avicenna born in Bukhara; his Canon of Medicine became the standard medical text in Europe and the Islamic world for six centuries.
Al-Biruni conducted pioneering work in astronomy, mathematics and comparative religion.
Rudaki, the father of Persian poetry, composed his masterpieces at the Samanid court.
Ferdowsi began composing the Shahnameh, the Persian national epic.
Distinctive Samanid pottery with elegant Kufic inscriptions and abstract designs.
Persian revived as a literary and administrative language alongside Arabic.
Sunni Islam promoted with the construction of madrasas and mosques.
Bukhara and Samarkand thrived as Silk Road centers connecting China to the Mediterranean.
Silver dirhams minted in vast quantities circulated across Eurasia.
The Persian cultural renaissance shaped all subsequent Islamic civilization.
The Samanid mausoleum in Bukhara remains a masterpiece of early Islamic architecture.

fall.text: The empire fell to the Turkic Kara-Khanids from the north and the Ghaznavids from the south.
